title: Bias & Fairness in ML
interviewAnswer: Bias can enter through sampling, labels, features, historical decisions or deployment feedback. Fairness has multiple incompatible definitions, so I first identify the affected groups and harm, then choose metrics/interventions aligned with the use case.
why: Aggregate accuracy can hide systematic harm or underperformance for a small group.
intuition: A model learns patterns in the data-generating process—including historical inequities and measurement errors—not an objective notion of fairness.
deepDive: Demographic parity, equalized odds and calibration answer different questions and cannot generally all hold simultaneously when base rates differ. Mitigations can occur in data, objectives, thresholds or workflow design.
workedExample: A hiring model with 90% overall accuracy may have much lower recall for one group because the historical labels reflect unequal opportunities.
commonMistakes: Choosing a fairness metric without defining the harm.
Removing protected attributes and assuming bias disappears.
followUps: How would you audit subgroup performance?
production: Continuously monitor subgroup distributions/outcomes where legally and ethically appropriate; changes in user populations can change fairness properties.
